About: Minkowski Metric Explorer

Source

Lecture
10 — Lorentz transformations
Simulation
1 — Minkowski space & metric (guided-inquiry); a (t, x) plane with a Local / Global zoom toggle.
Concept
The spacetime interval Δs² = −Δt² + Δx² (c = 1) defines a non-Euclidean "distance" that can be negative, zero, or positive — classifying event pairs as timelike, lightlike, or spacelike.
Serves
Describe Minkowski spacetime and its metric structure; identify invariant quantities under Lorentz transformations (the interval is the central invariant).
Inquiry
Place P₂ at spacelike / timelike / lightlike separations from P₁, read Δt and Δx off the grid, compute Δs², and watch the sign flip as the pair crosses the light cone.
Misconception
"A squared distance is always ≥ 0" — the Euclidean intuition. The Minkowski minus sign on the time term makes Δs² < 0 for timelike pairs.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict the sign of Δs²

Let’s start with two events. P₁ and P₂ sit on a (t, x) plane, with c = 1 so both axes carry light-seconds, and their separation is Δs² = −Δt² + Δx².

Now imagine P₂ moving from far out in space (Δx > Δt) to inside the dashed light cone (Δt > Δx). In Euclidean geometry a squared distance is never negative. So what do you think Δs² does along the way?

2 · A zero interval

Here’s a special case. P₂ now sits exactly on a dashed 45° line through P₁: Δt and Δx are equal, and neither is zero, so Δs² = 0. What do you think that zero says about this pair?

3 · Inside the cone

Now let’s step inside. P₂ has moved inside the dashed cone, where Δt is the larger of the two gaps and Δs² is negative. What do you think can connect this pair of events?

4 · What sets the length

One last experiment. A displacement of fixed coordinate length is turned through α, away from the t-axis, and the grey dashed step keeps the same length at every α. What do you think the coloured interval ds does as α passes 45°?

5 · The Minkowski metric

So here’s the big idea. The Minkowski metric η turns the two gaps into the interval, Δs² = −Δt² + Δx²: the time gap enters with a minus sign where the Euclidean rule d² = Δx² + Δy² has a plus.

EuclideanMinkowski
signnever negative+, 0 or −
zero whenthe points coincidelight connects the events

Every inertial observer computes the same Δs², so all agree which of the three cases a pair falls into. The curves of constant Δs² are hyperbolae, not circles, and a boost only slides an event along its hyperbola, never off it. When you’re ready, press Finish and explore freely.

Symbols & notation

▾
Δt, Δx — finite coordinate differences between P₁ and P₂ (light-seconds).
Δs² — finite squared interval = −Δt² + Δx² (ls²). The invariant interval: same in every inertial frame.
dt, dx — infinitesimal displacements (Local view). Symbols, not numbers.
ds² — infinitesimal squared interval = −dt² + dx².
ημν — Minkowski metric tensor, diag(−1, +1) in the (t, x) basis.
Signature (−, +), c = 1 ⇒ Δs² < 0 timelike, = 0 lightlike, > 0 spacelike.
c = 1 — time & space in the same units (light-seconds, "ls"). Spacetime interval: Δs² = −Δt² + Δx² (in ls²).
Spacetime interval (finite)
Metric tensor (infinitesimal form)
Classification
Proper time (timelike pairs)
Worked check points
Invariance
Δs² is a Lorentz-invariant scalar — all inertial observers compute the same value even though they disagree on Δt and Δx separately. (The next simulation demonstrates this under a Lorentz boost.)

The Physics

Minkowski space & the metric · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Two events, P₁ and P₂, sit on a space–time diagram. This sim computes one number for the pair, the interval Δs², and shows how that number relates to the light cone and to the length of a small step.

What you'll learn

  • How the interval Δs² is built from the time gap Δt and the space gap Δx.
  • How the sign of Δs² relates to the light cone.
  • What √|Δs²| measures, and for which pairs it can be measured.
  • How the metric sets the length of a step, and what happens to Δs² when the frame changes.
Two events and the gaps between them. P₂ opens at Δt = 3, Δx = 4.

03

The interval is a difference of squares

Δt and Δx are the time gap and the space gap between the two events, measured in one inertial frame: the frame of the grid. The interval combines them with opposite signs:

The interval Δs². With c = 1 it is −Δt² + Δx².
The same pair, P₂ at Δt = 3, Δx = 4. The Euclidean distance² adds the squares and is never negative. Δs² gives the time term a minus sign and can be negative.
Signature (−, +): timelike pairs are negative, lightlike pairs zero, spacelike pairs positive.
Key idea. Δs² is not a distance squared. Δt² counts as negative and Δx² as positive, so Δs² can be negative, zero or positive.
See itRead Δt = 3 and Δx = 4 off the grid and let the Compute box do the arithmetic. Watch for: the Compute line starting with −9.0, the time term, and ending in 7.0 ls².
04

The light cone sorts the pairs

The dashed lines through P₁ are the light cone: the points where |Δt| = |Δx|, which at c = 1 is exactly the path of light. Comparing |Δt| with |Δx| gives the sign.

The three cases.
  • Timelike (inside the cone): a signal slower than light can link the events.
  • Lightlike (on the cone): only light can link them.
  • Spacelike (outside): no signal can link them.
Examples: Δs² = −12 inside the cone, 0 on it, +7 outside. The sign of Δt separates future from past.

Δs² = 0 does not mean the same event. At Δt = 3, Δx = 3 the events are 3 ls apart and Δs² is still 0.

See itKeep Δt = 3 and slide P₂ from Δx = 5 in to Δx = 0. Watch for: the Compute line changing from positive to 0.0 at Δx = 3, then to negative.
See itPut P₂ on the cone at Δt = 3, Δx = 3. Watch for: P₂ sitting on a dashed line, with the photon dots running along that line.
05

What the interval measures

The square root of |Δs²|, by type.
  • Timelike: √(−Δs²) is the proper time (c = 1), what a single clock present at both events reads. That clock moves at speed |Δx/Δt| < 1.
  • Spacelike: √Δs² is the proper distance, the separation measured in a frame where the two events are simultaneous. No clock or signal links them.
  • Lightlike: Δs² = 0, so both roots are 0. Only a light signal links the events.
Δt Δx

These sliders move the sim too.

See itPut P₂ inside the cone at Δt = 4, Δx = 2. Watch for: the Compute line giving Δs² = −12.0 ls², so a clock between the events reads √12 ≈ 3.46 s.
06

The metric sets the length of a step

Local metric view takes one step (dt, dx) = (cos α, sin α), so its coordinate length √(dt² + dx²) is 1 for every α. The metric turns the step into an interval:

The metric η, with signature (−, +).

As α turns from the t-axis (0°) to the x-axis (90°), ds² goes from −1 through 0 at α = 45°, the light-cone direction, to +1. The coloured bar has length √|cos 2α|, so it is shortest at 45° and returns to 1 at 90°.

Key idea. The grid does not set the length of a step. The metric does.
See itTurn the step from α = 0° to 90°. Watch for: the coloured bar shrinking to a point at α = 45° (ds → 0), then growing again.
07

Why every observer agrees on Δs²

A second inertial frame S′, moving at speed v along x, assigns the same two events different gaps Δt′ and Δx′ (Lorentz transformation, c = 1):

Both gaps change; the difference of their squares does not.

So every inertial observer finds the same Δs², and the same type: timelike, lightlike or spacelike cannot depend on the frame. A rotation of the diagram would preserve Δt² + Δx² (circles). A boost preserves −Δt² + Δx² (hyperbolas).

P₂ at Δx = 4, Δt = 3, boosted by v = 0.5 c. It moves along the hyperbola, not the circle.

The sim has no moving frame. The boost is done on paper, and the sim shows the two resulting pairs.

See itBoost the pair Δt = 5, Δx = 3 by v = 0.6 c (γ = 1.25) on paper, to Δt′ = 4, Δx′ = 0. Watch for: the Compute line giving 16.0 ls² for both pairs.
08

Where it matters

  • Cause and effect. Only timelike or lightlike pairs can be linked by a signal. Since Δs² is the same in every frame, all observers agree which pairs those are.
  • Time order. For a timelike pair, every observer agrees which event comes first. For a spacelike pair, different frames can disagree, and the pair cannot be causally linked anyway.
  • Muons. Creation and decay of a muon form a timelike pair. √(−Δs²) is the muon's own mean lifetime, 2.2 μs. In the Earth frame at 0.99 c (γ ≈ 7.1) the time between the events is about 16 μs.
Go deeper: the same structure for energy and momentum
  • The energy–momentum pair (E, p) transforms like (t, x), and −E² + p² = −m² (c = 1) is its invariant, with the same signature (−, +).
  • A particle with m > 0 is timelike, a photon with m = 0 is lightlike.
09

Summary

In one line. Δs² = −Δt² + Δx² (c = 1) is the same in every inertial frame, and its sign sorts every pair of events as timelike, lightlike or spacelike.

Key points

  • √(−Δs²) is a proper time (timelike), √Δs² a proper distance (spacelike).
  • The metric, not the grid, sets the length of a step.
  • A change of inertial frame changes Δt and Δx but not Δs².

Common mix-ups

  • "A squared quantity can't be negative." Δs² is not a square of a real length. It is a difference of two squares.
  • "Δs² = 0 means the same event." It means the events lie on each other's light cone, which can be several ls apart.
  • "The interval is the length of the thick line on screen." The line is drawn on the Euclidean grid. Δs² is computed from Δt and Δx by the metric.

Things to try on your own

  • Read Δt and Δx off the grid, type them into the Compute box, and compare with the true values.
  • In Local view, find the angle other than 30° where the bar has the same length as at 30°.
  • Place P₂ at Δt = 5, Δx = 3, then at Δt = 4, Δx = 0, and compare Δs².
